title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
formal: Is the following computational impossibility statement true? For every fixed integer \(k\ge3\), rational \(0<\varepsilon<(k-2)/4\), and rational \(0<c<1\), no uniform randomized polynomial-time classical algorithm can, for all sufficiently large \(n\), recover a vector with absolute correlation at least \(c\) with a uniformly random hidden unit direction from the single rounded tensor observation \[Y=\lambda_n v^{\otimes k}+Z,\qquad \lambda_n=n^{k/4-\varepsilon},\qquad v\sim\operatorname{Unif}(S^{n-1}),\] where all \(n^k\) ordered entries of \(Z\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables. Recovery must succeed with probability at least \(2/3\), averaged over the hidden direction, noise and algorithm coins. Rounding, output normalization and the uniform bit-cost model are defined below. The fixed power saving \(n^\varepsilon\) and the spherical prior are parts of the existing target, not replaced by a threshold for one algorithm family.
definitions:
\(S^{n-1}=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i v_i^2=1\}\), with its rotation-invariant probability measure. A tensor is an array indexed by all ordered tuples \((i_1,\ldots,i_k)\in[n]^k\), including repeated indices. Its rank-one signal has entry \(\lambda_n v_{i_1}\cdots v_{i_k}\). The Gaussian noise entries, the direction and learner coins are independent. In particular the noise is not symmetrized: entries indexed by different permutations remain independent. The learner has exactly one tensor observation, with no labeled coordinates, informative starting vector, auxiliary graph or additional independent noise samples. The fixed constants \(k,\varepsilon,c\) are known to its program, but \(v\) and \(Z\) are hidden.

For \(n\ge2\), put \[b_n=\lceil10k\log_2 n\rceil,\qquad Q_b(x)=2^{-b}\left\lfloor2^b\max\{-2^b,\min\{x,2^b\}\}\right\rfloor.\] The actual input is \(n\) and the complete list \((Q_{b_n}(Y_{i_1,\ldots,i_k}))_{[n]^k}\) in lexicographic tuple order. Each entry is encoded by its signed integer numerator with the common denominator \(2^{b_n}\); the numerator has at most \(2b_n+2\) bits. The clipping interval and rounding direction are fixed, not chosen adaptively by the algorithm. The exact real tensor exists only in the sampling experiment; the machine receives no oracle for its discarded digits. The input length is \(O(n^k\log n)\) at fixed \(k\). This is the previously adopted explicit finite-precision version of the Gaussian question, not a theorem asserting equivalence to every exact-real formulation.

An allowed algorithm is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with independent fair random bits. There exist constants \(B,a\ge1\), possibly depending on the fixed triple, such that it terminates within \(Bn^a\) bit operations on every encoded input of this dimension and every random tape. Reading, storage operations, arithmetic, writing the output and its rational encodings are included. The single program and polynomial work for all \(n\), with no advice depending on dimension. Since \(k\) is fixed, this is polynomial in the complete input length. There are no exact-real or quantum operations.

The output is a list of \(n\) rational coordinates \(w_i\), each a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. A malformed vector or \(w=0\) fails. Otherwise interpret \(u=w/\|w\|_2\), where \(\langle w,v\rangle=\sum_i w_i v_i\) and \(\|w\|_2=(\sum_i w_i^2)^{1/2}\). The success event is the mathematically defined inequality \[|\langle w,v\rangle|\ge c\|w\|_2.\] The learner need not compute that event, since it does not know the planted direction. Absolute correlation permits a global sign flip, including the inherent even-order ambiguity. The output need not encode the irrational normalized vector exactly; its rational representative determines the direction.

Write \(p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)\) for the probability of this event in the specified experiment. The target is \[\forall(k,\varepsilon,c)\ \forall A\text{ of polynomial bit cost}\ \forall N\ge2\ \exists n\ge N:\quad p_A(n;k,\varepsilon,c)<2/3.\] Thus the conjecture rules out eventual success on all dimensions; it does not claim that every algorithm fails at every large dimension, or that its success probability must tend to zero. Conversely, a refutation needs one fixed triple and one machine with eventual success at least \(2/3\). The range of \(\varepsilon\) ensures \(\lambda_n/\sqrt n=n^{(k-2)/4-\varepsilon}\to\infty\), placing the signal above the usual statistical scale in the unrounded model.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the full quantified impossibility statement, or a Lean-verified counterexample consisting of one fixed triple, a single algorithm, polynomial worst-case bit/output bounds and an \(N\) for which \(p_A(n)\ge2/3\) for every \(n\ge N\). A lower bound against low-degree estimators, one iterative method, or a different prior is not the universal statement. Detection and recovery must not be interchanged without a proved reduction. Any normalization, symmetrization, multiple-sample or precision transfer must be justified in the same success and resource model. A conditional hardness reduction is partial progress until its premise is proved. Logarithmic threshold improvements or a constant-prefactor improvement at \(n^{k/4}\) do not supply the fixed exponent saving. The desired output quality is a fixed absolute correlation, not coordinatewise numerical recovery.
why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

importance.reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.

progress.text: Montanari–Richard introduce and analyze the spiked tensor model, exhibiting a gap between information-theoretic recovery and the analyzed polynomial-time methods.
Kunisky–Moore–Wein prove spherical-prior low-degree detection thresholds and odd-order reconstruction lower bounds with the predicted dependence on degree.
Wu–Zhou sharpen the analysis and stopping rule for randomly initialized power iteration; its threshold improves by a polylogarithmic factor.
Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang improve stochastic-gradient guarantees in a multiple-observation model; the even-order bound reaches the familiar conjectured computational scale.
Fu–Sohn establish low-degree estimation bounds for independent-coordinate priors, with the predicted degree–signal dependence and an additional technical restriction on degree.
A smooth constant-prefactor transition is proved for Rademacher-spike tensor PCA; the runtime exponent depends on the fixed prefactor.
Average-case reductions connect planted XOR and Boolean-spike tensor PCA while retaining hardness premises and parameter/model restrictions.
A detection-focused acceleration paper includes a spectral-property caveat and does not give a proved recovery theorem at the requested signal.
Rechecked priors, normalization, precision and leading exponents; kept the full finite-bit spherical recovery conjecture and distinguished power iteration’s separate threshold.

status_note: No checked result through16 September2026 settles the displayed unrestricted finite-bit spherical recovery statement. The 2024 cumulant reconstruction theorem is restricted to odd order and low-degree estimators; the May2026 general-prior result assumes independent coordinates and both of its degree conditions. Random-start power iteration has scale n^{(k−1)/2}, while multiple-observation gradient and constant-prefactor critical-scale improvements do not produce a fixed power saving below n^{k/4}. The 2026 XOR reductions use Boolean spikes and conditional hardness premises. The checked Hastings2026 paper proves detection guarantees with a stated spectral-property caveat, not this recovery theorem. All such results remain context, and unrounded-to-rounded equivalence is not claimed.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order \(\sqrt{n}\). Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order \(\sqrt{n}\) here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around \(n^{k/4}\), up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from \(\sqrt{n}\). The interval for \(\varepsilon\) deliberately places our target strictly between them: \(\lambda /\sqrt{n}=n^{(k- 2)/4- \varepsilon}\) grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Randomly initialized power iteration has a different benchmark from the best known general methods: Wu–Zhou analyze its scale \(n^{(k-1)/2}\) and improve it by a polylogarithmic factor. For \(k\ge3\), this is a larger leading exponent than \(k/4\). That algorithm-specific improvement is not an improvement below the card’s general computational threshold.

Ding–Gu–Liu–Fang study \(N\) independent observations and a normalized stochastic-gradient method, with a sufficient condition \(N\lambda^2\ge\widetilde\Omega(n^{\lceil k/2\rceil})\). For even order, normalizing the average to variance-one Gaussian noise gives signal strength \(\sqrt N\lambda\) at the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale. Their theorem neither proves an unrestricted lower bound nor supplies this card’s fixed power saving from one observation.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

Li’s 2025 theorem reaches a constant-prefactor critical scale for a Rademacher spike and symmetric noise, with a polynomial exponent depending on that fixed prefactor. After normalizing a sign vector to unit length, the leading signal exponent is \(k/4\). Replacing a fixed prefactor by \(n^{-\varepsilon}\) is not justified by a theorem whose runtime exponent depends on it. The spike prior also differs from the sphere.

The 2026 Bresler–Harbuzova reductions connect noisy planted XOR problems with Boolean-spike tensor PCA and transport algorithms or hardness hypotheses between parameter regimes. They preserve and compare conjectured barriers; they do not prove an unconditional barrier for the spherical prior or eliminate the specified finite-precision interface.

Hastings’s February2026 paper concerns detection rather than a proved recovery guarantee. Its added note also withdraws an unqualified provable speedup comparison after a sharper spectral-norm bound became known, retaining a spectral-property condition. It does not settle this classical recovery statement.

upgraded_from.title: The computational threshold for dense tensor PCA

sentences: The card asks whether every efficient classical algorithm fails to recover constant correlation with a hidden spherical direction below a specified tensor-PCA signal scale.
Its observation is one fully listed tensor with independent ordered Gaussian noise, fixed finite-precision rounding and no extra information.
The statement precisely separates failure on arbitrarily large dimensions from the eventual-success counterexample needed to refute it.
Recent low-degree, power-iteration, multiple-observation and threshold-refinement results retain model or resource restrictions.
A Lean resolution must handle the full uniform bit model and its exact spherical recovery probability, preserving all normalization and precision choices.
